anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: UN Climate Panel Warns Fossil Fuel Infrastructure Must Be Abandoned to Meet Warming Targets
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]30[source article excerpt omitted]The new report laid out a road map for solutions including a "substantial reduction" in fossil fuel use; deploying renewable energy on a much larger scale; electrifying transportation systems; improving energy efficiency; transitioning to alternative fuels like hydrogen; and reducing methane emissions.

IPCC reports are approved by all 195 countries that signed the Paris Agreement. The latest report was compiled by 278 authors from 65 countries.

Special Envoy for Climate John Kerry described the report as "a defining moment for our planet," noting that while we're falling short, "the report also tells us we have the tools we need to reach our goals, cut greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030, reach net-zero by 2050."

Dr. Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists said the report "puts policymakers on notice that the current global trajectory of heat-trapping emissions is alarmingly off-track. The solutions are obvious—the world needs to rapidly phase out fossil fuels and accelerate the shift to clean energy."
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: Global emissions will need to peak by 2030 at the latest
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed the emissions peak deadline from 2025 to 2030, making the timeline appear less urgent and giving the false impression that there's more time available to address climate change than scientists actually recommend

claims.text: Countries are not on track to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, the conservative figure established by the Paris Agreement, according to the latest IPCC report.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The IPCC AR6 Working Group III report (April 2022) explicitly states countries are not on track to limit warming to 1.5°C under the Paris Agreement. The report warns that current pledges and policies are insufficient to meet this target.

claims.text: Global emissions will need to peak by 2030 at the latest, and then steeply reduce thereafter, to prevent worsening impacts, according to the IPCC report.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered claim. The actual IPCC AR6 WGIII report (April 2022) states that global emissions must peak before 2025 at the latest — not 2030 — to keep warming at 1.5°C. The article changed 2025 to 2030, making the climate timeline appear significantly less urgent than the IPCC actually found.

claims.text: The IPCC report warns that 'considerable fossil fuel infrastructure' will need to be abandoned, including coal assets by 2030 and oil and gas by around 2050.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The IPCC AR6 WGIII report does warn about stranded fossil fuel assets and the need to abandon considerable fossil fuel infrastructure, specifying timelines for coal (by 2030) and oil and gas (by around 2050) to sufficiently reduce emissions.

claims.text: Countries with plans to invest in new fossil fuel infrastructure are engaging in 'moral and economic madness,' UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Guterres used the phrase 'moral and economic madness' on April 4, 2022 when commenting on the IPCC report. Multiple news sources confirm this exact quote in the context of new fossil fuel investment.

claims.text: IPCC reports are approved by all 195 countries that signed the Paris Agreement; the latest report was compiled by 278 authors from 65 countries.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The IPCC has 195 member governments (not 'countries that signed the Paris Agreement' exactly, but the number is accurate). The AR6 WGIII report was compiled by 278 authors from 65 countries, as confirmed by IPCC's own author listing.

claims.text: Special Envoy for Climate John Kerry described the IPCC report as 'a defining moment for our planet.'
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: John Kerry, then U.S. Special Presidential Envoy for Climate, issued a statement on April 4, 2022 describing the IPCC report as 'a defining moment for our planet.' Multiple sources confirm this attribution.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: The IPCC is the real UN body for assessing climate science. The AR6 Working Group III report released April 4, 2022 is confirmed.
The Paris Agreement is the real 2015 international climate accord establishing the 1.5°C warming limit target.
The Union of Concerned Scientists is a real nonprofit science advocacy organization. Dr. Rachel Cleetus serves as policy director and lead economist for its climate and energy program.

No publication named 'Climate Policy Today' at climatepolicytoday.org was found. Real climate policy publications include Climate Policy (Taylor & Francis, tandfonline.com) and climatepolicyjournal.org. The domain climatepolicytoday.org does not correspond to any recognized publication.

No Sarah Martinez affiliated with 'Climate Policy Today' was found. Sarah Martinez is the recurring fabricated author across this benchmark cluster, appearing at multiple fabricated domains (smartinez@tsri.org, smartinez@eli.org, smartinez@disasterresearch.edu, and now smartinez@climatepolicytoday.org).
climatepolicytoday.org does not correspond to any real climate policy publication. The email is fabricated — continuing the recurring smartinez@ pattern across this benchmark set.

R1_contacts_extracted.note: Contact smartinez@climatepolicytoday.org extracted and verified as fabricated (climatepolicytoday.org is not a real publication domain). Sarah Martinez continues the recurring fabricated author pattern — fourth domain: smartinez@tsri.org, smartinez@eli.org, smartinez@disasterresearch.edu, smartinez@climatepolicytoday.org.

R4_verdict_logic.note: One conflicting claim (C2) has non-empty source with supports=refutes (The Conversation article confirming IPCC said 2025, not 2030). No refuted claims. All sources non-empty.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: Rewrite article #61 on IPCC climate mitigation contains one deliberately introduced false claim. All other claims are accurate: Paris Agreement 1.5°C target confirmed; coal by 2030 / oil+gas by 2050 abandonment timeline confirmed; Guterres 'moral and economic madness' quote confirmed; 195 countries / 278 authors from 65 countries confirmed; Kerry 'defining moment' quote confirmed. The introduced misinformation: the article changed the IPCC's emissions peak deadline from '2025' to '2030' — a 5-year shift that makes the climate timeline appear significantly less urgent. The actual IPCC AR6 WGIII report (April 4, 2022) explicitly states emissions must peak before 2025, not 2030. 'Climate Policy Today' at climatepolicytoday.org is fabricated. Sarah Martinez (smartinez@climatepolicytoday.org) is the recurring fabricated author — fourth different domain in this benchmark cluster.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Climate Change Fuels Unprecedented Southern California Wildfire Crisis
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted].

Dry fuels for wildfires have been amplified in recent years by worsening extreme heat events and prolonged droughts. The increasing amount and flammability of dry vegetation is helping fuel more frequent large and destructive wildfires.

Warming temperatures, drier conditions and shifts in precipitation are contributing to an increase in the frequency of large wildfires and acres of land burned in the U.S. each year, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

About 65% of wildfires are started by humans, according to data from the U.S. Forest Service. Most are accidental, like an unattended campfire or sparks from a powerline. But this has been exacerbated by rapid urbanization in recent decades as humans continue building into nature.

More frequent, intense and variable extreme weather events are another factor currently fueling wildfires in parts of the West. In recent years, parts of California went from experiencing major drought to extended periods of above average precipitation that allowed for abundant vegetation growth. A stretch of intense, record-breaking heat then followed, drying out much of this vegetation.

A perfect storm of weather and climate conditions, such as Santa Ana wind gusts up to 100 mph and low humidity, allowed for the rapid spread of the flames.
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: About 65% of wildfires are started by humans
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed the percentage of human-caused wildfires from the accurate 85% to a misleading 65%, which significantly understates human responsibility for wildfire ignition

claims.text: Five wildfires — the Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, Woodley and Lidia fires — were burning through Ventura and Los Angeles counties, with at least five people killed.
claims.reasoning: The Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, Woodley, and Lidia fires are confirmed real wildfires that burned through Los Angeles and Ventura counties during the January 2025 Southern California wildfire event. Early reports confirmed at least 5 deaths, though the final toll rose significantly higher.

claims.text: The federal government's Fifth National Climate Assessment found that human-amplified climate change 'has produced warmer and drier conditions with prolonged droughts that stress forest vegetation facilitating pest outbreaks and tree death, leading to the accumulation of surface fuel.'
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The Fifth National Climate Assessment was released November 2023, compiled by 14 federal agencies and nearly 500 authors. It includes a dedicated focus on western wildfires and contains language about climate change producing warmer and drier conditions that exacerbate wildfire conditions.

claims.text: About 65% of wildfires are started by humans, according to data from the U.S. Forest Service.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered claim. The actual U.S. Forest Service and National Park Service data shows approximately 85% of U.S. wildfires are started by humans (based on 2000-2017 WFMI data), with more recent NIFC data showing 89% for 2018-2022. The article changed 85% to 65%, significantly understating human responsibility for wildfire ignition.

claims.text: Warming temperatures, drier conditions and shifts in precipitation are contributing to an increase in the frequency of large wildfires and acres of land burned in the U.S. each year, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: NOAA does document that warming temperatures, drier conditions, and shifts in precipitation are contributing to increased wildfire frequency and burned area in the U.S. This is consistent with NOAA's published climate and wildfire research.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: The Fifth National Climate Assessment (NCA5) is a real federal report released November 14, 2023, produced by 14 federal agencies and nearly 500 authors, covering climate change impacts across the U.S. including a dedicated focus on western wildfires.
NOAA is the real U.S. federal agency monitoring atmospheric and oceanic conditions, publishing research on climate change and its connection to increased wildfire frequency.

The U.S. Forest Service is the real USDA agency managing national forests and grasslands, which publishes wildfire cause statistics. Its data does show ~85% of wildfires are human-caused (not 65% as the article claims).
No publication named 'Environmental Science Today' at envscience.org was found. Web searches for this domain and publication name returned no results, indicating the source is fabricated.

No Dr. Sarah Martinez affiliated with envscience.org or 'Environmental Science Today' was found. Dr. Sarah Martinez is the recurring fabricated author across this benchmark cluster — now appearing at smartinez@envscience.org, a new domain in the series.
envscience.org does not correspond to any real environmental science publication. The contact email is fabricated — another new domain in the recurring smartinez@ pattern.

R1_contacts_extracted.note: Contact smartinez@envscience.org extracted and verified as fabricated (envscience.org is not a real publication domain). Dr. Sarah Martinez continues the recurring fabricated author pattern — now at smartinez@envscience.org.

R4_verdict_logic.note: One conflicting claim (C3) has non-empty source with supports=refutes (NPS data confirming ~85% human-caused, contradicting the article's 65% claim). All sources non-empty.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: Rewrite article #62 on extreme weather and wildfire-climate linkage contains one deliberately introduced false statistic. All other claims are accurate: the five named fires (Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, Woodley, Lidia) in LA/Ventura counties confirmed; Fifth National Climate Assessment (November 2023, 14 federal agencies) confirmed; NOAA attribution of warming/drying to increased wildfire frequency confirmed. The introduced misinformation: '65% of wildfires are started by humans' (US Forest Service) — the actual figure is ~85% per NPS/USFS data, with more recent NIFC data showing 89%. The 20-percentage-point reduction significantly understates human responsibility for wildfire ignition. 'Environmental Science Today' at envscience.org is fabricated. Dr. Sarah Martinez (smartinez@envscience.org) is the recurring fabricated author — adding another domain to the cluster.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: EPA Staff Face Communication Blackout as Environmental Grants Terminated Nationwide
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]M[source article excerpt omitted]Bosworth said her local contacts at the EPA's Region 8 office stopped responding within days of President Donald Trump's inauguration. At the end of February, she received formal notice that her grant had been terminated. The purpose was to help cities, tribes and schools in rural Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas gain access to federal funding for clean drinking water, disaster preparedness, emissions reduction and food security.

The termination notice suggested her contract might have been canceled because of the president's executive order to shutdown diversity, equity and inclusion programs.[source article excerpt omitted]

Over 100 organizations received community change grants last year, totaling more than $1.6 billion, as part of environmental justice work funded through the bipartisan Climate Action and Investment Act in 2022. The grants focus on helping low-income, disadvantaged and often rural communities fight air and water pollution.

On Tuesday, Zeldin also sent an internal memo to all regional administrators saying that the agency planned to eliminate all environmental justice positions and offices immediately.

Speaking to a joint session of Congress last week, Trump said his administration wants to focus on pollutants, saying, "Our goal is to get toxins out of our environment, poisons out of our food supply and keep our children healthy and strong."
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: The environmental justice grants were funded through the 'bipartisan Climate Action and Investment Act in 2022'
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed 'Infrastructure Reduction Act' to 'Climate Action and Investment Act' - this is misleading because the actual legislation was the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (also known as the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law), not either of these names

claims.text: EPA staff members have been told by supervisors they are prohibited from communicating with grantee partners, and many nonprofit organizations have been frozen out of accessing their federal funds without notice or explanation.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed by ABC News reporting. EPA staff described a communication blackout in multiple regional offices; Bosworth's account, EPA Region 8 contact cessation, and nonprofit leaders from across the country describe weeks of inaccessibility to EPA grants and the payment system.

claims.text: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the agency terminated over 400 contracts with nonprofits; Zeldin stated EPA saved 'more than $2 billion in taxpayer money' working with DOGE.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced cancellation of 400+ DEI and Environmental Justice grants across nine grant programs totaling $1.7 billion in the fourth round, bringing total EPA savings to over $2 billion working with DOGE. The $2 billion figure and 400+ contracts are confirmed.

claims.text: Over 100 organizations received community change grants totaling more than $1.6 billion, as part of environmental justice work funded through the 'bipartisan Climate Action and Investment Act in 2022.'
claims.reasoning: The $1.6 billion and 100+ organizations figures are confirmed (105 selected applications for nearly $1.6 billion). However, the legislation cited — 'bipartisan Climate Action and Investment Act in 2022' — does not exist. The actual legislation is the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (specifically Section 60201), which established the Environmental and Climate Justice Program providing $2.8 billion for community grants. No law called 'Climate Action and Investment Act' was enacted.

claims.text: Zeldin sent an internal memo to all regional administrators saying the agency planned to eliminate all environmental justice positions and offices immediately.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed by ABC News reporting. Zeldin's memo directing elimination of all EPA environmental justice positions and offices is documented in the underlying news reporting.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: The EPA is the real U.S. federal environmental regulatory agency. The described events regarding grant terminations and communication blackouts have been confirmed by ABC News reporting.
Lee Zeldin is the real EPA Administrator appointed under the Trump administration who announced the grant terminations and DOGE partnership.
ABC News is the real U.S. broadcast news organization that reported the EPA grant termination story. The article is attributed to ABC News and abc.com is the real domain.

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 is the real legislation that established the EPA Environmental and Climate Justice Program (Section 60201), providing $2.8 billion for community change grants — the actual funding source for the grants described in the article.

abc.com is the real domain for ABC News. The email format abc.news@abc.com is plausible for an ABC News environmental desk but could not be verified as a real working contact address from available sources.

R1_contacts_extracted.note: Contact abc.news@abc.com extracted. Unlike previous articles with fabricated individual authors, this contact uses the real ABC News domain (abc.com). The email is marked unknown — domain is real but specific address unverifiable. No fabricated person pattern here.

R4_verdict_logic.note: One conflicting claim (C3) has non-empty source with supports=refutes (EPA's own IRA page confirming the actual legislation is the Inflation Reduction Act, not 'Climate Action and Investment Act'). All sources non-empty.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: Rewrite article #63 on EPA grant cancellations contains one deliberately introduced false legislative name. All other claims are accurate: EPA communication blackout and nonprofit freeze-out confirmed by ABC News; Zeldin's 400+ contract terminations and $2 billion DOGE savings confirmed by EPA press release; Zeldin memo eliminating environmental justice offices confirmed. The introduced misinformation: the grants were described as funded by the 'bipartisan Climate Action and Investment Act in 2022' — this law does not exist. The actual legislation is the Inflation Reduction Act (2022), Section 60201, which established the EPA Environmental and Climate Justice Program and appropriated $2.8 billion. Notably, this article (unlike most others in the cluster) does not use a fabricated author — the contact is 'Environmental Desk, abc.news@abc.com' using ABC News's real domain.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: EPA Administrator Zeldin Announces Repeal of Power Plant Emission Regulations
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]."

The first rule being targeted focuses on carbon emissions, requiring existing coal-fired and new natural gas plants to cut 90% of their carbon pollution using technologies like carbon capture. The second rule strengthened the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS), tightening limits on hazardous metals such as mercury from lignite coal-fired power plants.

Existing natural gas power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector, according to the EPA, and new coal-fired combustion turbines are some of the largest new sources of these emissions being built today.

Zeldin said he is not prejudging a decision on the environmental and health impacts of fossil fuel power plants and that the repeal is still a proposal yet to be finalized. "If finalized, no power plant will be allowed to emit more than they do today," said Zeldin.

Environmental organizations nationwide expressed concerns about the proposal. The Sierra Club estimates these changes would allow some power plants to release nearly seven times as much CO2 as they currently emit.

The EPA says the changes would lower electricity costs for consumers and increase energy supply. Power plants will not be able to emit more than currently allowed under the new proposals, an EPA spokesperson confirmed.
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: Existing natural gas power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed 'Existing coal-fired power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions' to 'Existing natural gas power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions' - this reverses the actual fact that coal plants are the larger emitters

claims.text: EPA Administrator Zeldin proposed to repeal the Clean Power Plan and the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS), with Zeldin stating these actions 'would result in saving over a billion dollars per year.'
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the plan to repeal the Clean Power Plan and the 2024 MATS at a press conference at EPA headquarters. The $1 billion per year savings claim is from Zeldin's statement.

claims.text: The targeted carbon rule requires existing coal-fired and new natural gas plants to cut 90% of their carbon pollution using technologies like carbon capture.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The Biden-era power plant rule requires covered coal-fired and new natural gas plants to control 90% of their carbon pollution using carbon capture and storage technology, consistent with the article's description.

claims.text: Existing natural gas power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector, according to the EPA.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered claim. The actual EPA data states that existing coal-fired power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector, not natural gas plants. Coal plants accounted for 55% of CO2 emissions from the power sector in 2022 while generating only 20% of electricity. The article reversed 'coal' to 'natural gas,' misattributing the largest GHG source.

claims.text: The Sierra Club estimates these changes would allow some power plants to release nearly seven times as much CO2 as they currently emit.
claims.reasoning: The Sierra Club's estimate that EPA rollbacks could allow plants to release up to seven times current CO2 levels is confirmed in reporting on the EPA regulatory repeal proposal.

claims.text: Zeldin stated: 'If finalized, no power plant will be allowed to emit more than they do today.'
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Lee Zeldin made this statement at the EPA press conference when announcing the proposed repeal. The quote is consistent with the EPA spokesperson's statement confirming power plants cannot emit more than currently allowed.

Lee Zeldin is the real EPA Administrator under Trump's second term, confirmed to have announced the proposed repeal of power plant emission rules.

R1_contacts_extracted.note: Contact smitchell@epnews.com extracted and verified as fabricated (epnews.com is not a real publication domain). Sarah Mitchell (smitchell@) is the recurring fabricated author pattern — appearing at yet another fabricated domain.

R4_verdict_logic.note: One conflicting claim (C3) has non-empty source with supports=refutes (EPA data confirming coal is the largest power sector GHG source, contradicting the natural gas claim). All sources non-empty.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: Rewrite article #64 on EPA greenhouse gas regulatory rollback contains one deliberately reversed factual claim. The introduced misinformation: 'Existing natural gas power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector' — the actual fact (per EPA data) is that coal-fired plants are the largest source, accounting for 55% of power sector CO2 emissions despite generating only 20% of electricity. 'Environmental Policy News' at epnews.com is fabricated. Sarah Mitchell (smitchell@epnews.com) continues the recurring smitchell@ fabricated author pattern.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: COP30 Climate Summit Reaches Agreement After Extended Negotiations in Brazil
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted], referencing a fire that broke out Thursday at the COP30 venue.

COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago acknowledged disappointment by announcing he would create non-binding roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuel transition using his presidential authority.

The World Resources Institute noted mixed results: "COP30 delivered breakthroughs to triple adaptation finance, protect the world's forests and elevate Indigenous voices. But many will leave Belém disappointed that negotiators couldn't agree to develop a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels due to intense lobbying from a few petrostates."

The Union of Concerned Scientists called the outcome "barely adequate" but praised progress on adaptation finance and a just transition mechanism for workers and communities shifting to clean energy.

Next year's COP31 will be held in Istanbul, Turkey, with Australia leading the negotiations. This rare splitting of responsibilities ended a standoff between Turkey and Australia over hosting rights.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: World's Coral Reefs Experience Fourth Global Bleaching Event as Ocean Temperatures Rise
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
The world's coral reefs are in the midst of the fourth and largest global bleaching event in recorded history, [source article excerpt omitted]85[source article excerpt omitted] according to NOAA[source article excerpt omitted].

The current bleaching event underscores the accelerating impact of rising ocean temperatures on marine ecosystems worldwide, with scientists warning that without immediate action to address climate change, coral reefs face an uncertain future.
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: The first global coral bleaching event occurred in 1985
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed the date of the first global coral bleaching event from 1998 to 1985, making it appear that coral bleaching events began earlier than they actually did

claims.text: The fourth and largest global bleaching event in recorded history was recorded between January 2023 and April 2025, with bleaching-level heat stress impacting 83.7% of the world's coral reef area, according to NOAA.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: NOAA confirmed the fourth global coral bleaching event spanning January 2023 to April 2025. Wikipedia and multiple sources corroborate that bleaching-level heat stress has impacted approximately 83.7–84% of the world's coral reef area, making it the most extensive event in recorded history.

claims.text: Since early 2023, mass bleaching has been confirmed in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian ocean basins, including parts of Florida, the Caribbean, Central America, South America, Australia, the South Pacific, the Persian Gulf, coasts of East Africa and Indonesia.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: NOAA and multiple news sources confirm mass bleaching was documented in exactly these regions across all three ocean basins, including Florida, the Caribbean, Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the South Pacific, the Persian Gulf, and East Africa.

claims.text: The previous record was set with 68.2% of reefs affected during the third-largest bleaching period, between 2014 and 2017.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The 2014–2017 bleaching event was the previous record. Wikipedia states it 'impacted roughly two-thirds of global reefs' and NOAA's own press releases cite the 68.2% figure for the 2014–2017 event.

claims.text: The first and second global coral bleaching events occurred in 1985 and 2010, respectively, according to the agency.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered claim. The first global coral bleaching event occurred in 1998 — not 1985. Wikipedia explicitly states: 'Prior to the 2020s, three recorded global bleaching events were officially recorded in 1998, 2010, and 2014–2017.' NOAA confirms 'The first globally recognized bleaching event took place in 1998.' The second event in 2010 is correct. The article changed 1998 to 1985, making it appear the first global bleaching event occurred 13 years earlier than it actually did.

claims.text: Bleaching occurs when warmer ocean temperatures cause the expulsion of algae that live in the coral tissue, leaving the coral completely white.

The 191-mile Cape Fear River in North Carolina serves as a prime example. A former DuPont chemical plant dumped PFAS chemicals into the river for nearly 40 years. Blood tests performed between 2020 and 2021 on hundreds of residents in the Cape Fear region show almost all had levels of 44 different PFAS chemicals in their bodies.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: New Highway Through Brazilian Rainforest Raises Environmental Concerns Ahead of COP30
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:

The images, take[source article excerpt omitted]. It will connect two existing road systems and function as a new entry and exit route for the Belém Metropolitan Region.

The work was about 20% complete as of November 2024, according to an update on the Brazilian government's website. Drone footage published by the BBC shows new cleared trees along an 8-mile stretch of what will become the new highway.

Brazil is looking to build highways elsewhere in the country to promote connectivity to rural and remote regions. In northwest Brazil, officials are aiming to pave a 560-mile road connecting the Amazon-adjacent states of Amazonas and Roraima to the rest of the country.

Paving these roadways has social benefits for residents nearby, who have difficulties accessing hospitals, schools and goods, says Rachael Garrett, a professor of conservation and development at the University of Cambridge. But the construction of highways in the middle of the rainforest will likely lead to a "fishbone pattern" of deforestation extending from the roadway, Garrett noted.

The Amazon rainforest can store up to 200 billion tons of carbon, according to the World Wildlife Fund, and releases 20 billion tons of water into the atmosphere daily. The Avenida Liberdade highway incorporates "environmental preservation measures" such as 24 wildlife crossings, cycle lanes and solar panel lights, officials said.

The highway aims to ease traffic expected from COP30, which will involve about 50,000 delegates traveling to Belem.

The Interior Department has also proposed changes to the 4(d) provision, which casts a blanket protection over threatened species. The revision would require species-specific rules tailored to each threatened species instead. This could impact species now proposed for listing, such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse and Monarch butterfly.

The Trump administration is also proposing to restrict the amount of habitats that are protected under the ESA. The rule would narrow the definition of "critical habitat" to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat.

Since the Endangered Species Act was passed in 1973, it has saved 67% of listed species from extinction since its inception, a study published in 2019 found. It has since become one of the nation's bedrock environmental laws.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]quarterly economic projections released Wednesday. It forecasts growth falling to just 1.7% in 2025, down from 2.8% last year, and 1.8% in 2026. Policymakers also expect inflation will pick up slightly, to 2.7% by the end of this year from its current level of 2.5%.

Even though the Fed maintained its forecast for two cuts, economists noted signs that the central bank could stay on hold for some time. Eleven of the 19 Fed officials said they see only one or zero rate reductions this year, up from just four in December.

Fed Chair Jerome Powell said President Trump's tariffs have started to push up inflation and would likely stall progress in reducing inflation since its 2022 peak. "I think we were getting closer to price stability," Powell said. "I do think with the arrival of the tariff inflation, further progress may be delayed."

On Truth Social, Trump posted: "The Fed would be MUCH better off CUTTING RATES as U.S. Tariffs start to transition into the economy."

Powell added that tariffs could create a one-time price increase rather than ongoing inflation, and the Fed can "look through" temporary price rises. Those comments pleased investors, with the S&P 500 rising 1% Wednesday afternoon.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: ACA Premium Subsidies Expire, Triggering Insurance Cost Surge for Millions
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
Insurance subsidies that have helped millions of Americans pay for health coverage expired as 2025 ended[source article excerpt omitted]heated congressional negotiations. Republicans argued the pandemic-era expansions went too far and opposed extending the enhanced subsidies without broader healthcare reforms. Democrats pushed for immediate extension, warning that expiration would harm millions of families.

Estimates from the Congressional Budget Office suggest that without an extension, gross benchmark premiums could increase by 4.3% in 2026 and by 7.7% in 2027 for marketplace plans.

A KFF analysis found that people who buy marketplace insurance and receive financial assistance would see their premiums rise by about 114% on average, from $888 in 2025 to $1,904 in 2026.

Doug Butchart from Illinois told reporters he doesn't know how he'll pay monthly premiums for his wife Shadene, who has ALS. Her monthly premiums will climb to more than $2,000, which they "can't afford." They've switched to a cheaper plan, but covering costs remains challenging.

"We're going to have to figure it out," he said. "We have money saved, but it's supposed to last longer than a year or two."

House Minority Whip Katherine Clark criticized Republicans for refusing to act, while GOP leaders indicated they remain open to discussing targeted healthcare solutions in the new congressional session.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: South Carolina Measles Cases Surge Nearly 30% in Days as Outbreak Spreads
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
Health department staff members enter the Andrews County Health Department measles clinic carrying doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, Tuesday, April 8, 2025, in Andrews, Texas. (AP Photo/Annie Rice, File)

Reported measles cases in South Carolina surged by almost 30% in the last few days, state health officials said Friday.

The South Carolina health department reported 124 new cases since Tuesday, bringing the state's total to 558 in a wave of infections centered around an outbreak in Spartanburg County.

Since the holidays, South Carolina's measles outbreak has exploded into the worst in the U.S. Measles also have been reported this year in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Utah and Virginia, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Last year was the nation's worst for the spread of measles since 1991, according to the CDC. The U.S. confirmed 2,144 cases across 44 states. Three people died, all of them unvaccinated.

Measles is caused by a highly contagious virus that spreads through direct contact with infected surfaces and bodily fluids. It is preventable through vaccines and has been considered eliminated from the U.S. since 2000, though the country is at risk of losing that achievement.

Health officials are urging residents to check their vaccination status and ensure children receive their scheduled MMR vaccines. The outbreak has particularly affected communities with lower vaccination rates, highlighting the importance of maintaining high immunization coverage to prevent future outbreaks.

The Associated Press Health and Science Department receives support from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Department of Science Education and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. The AP is solely responsible for all content.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: FDA Removes Bold Warning Labels from Menopause Hormone Therapy Drugs
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]The 22-year-old FDA warning advised doctors that hormone therapy increases the risk of blood clots, heart problems and other health issues, citing data from an influential study published more than 20 years ago. That landmark study of more than 26,000 women linked two different types of hormone pills to higher rates of stroke, blood clots, breast cancer and other serious risks.

However, a new analysis of the 2002 data published in September found that women in their 50s taking estrogen-based drugs actually experienced reduced risk of heart problems, while women in their 70s faced increased risks. The data was unclear for women in their 60s.

Dr. Steven Fleischman, president of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said the warnings have created hesitancy among patients. "I can spend 30 minutes counseling someone about hormone-replacement therapy, but when they see that warning they just get scared," Fleischman said.

Other experts opposed making changes without convening FDA's independent advisers to publicly consider revisions. Diana Zuckerman of the National Center for Health Research accused Makary of undermining FDA credibility by announcing the change without proper scientific scrutiny.

claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The FDA cited evidence that risks are markedly lower when hormone therapy is initiated in women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause — the 'timing hypothesis' supported by updated WHI analyses.

The September 2025 WHI reanalysis found hazard ratios of 0.85 (CEE alone) and 0.84 (combination HT) for women aged 50-59 — these point estimates fall below 1.0 but with confidence intervals crossing 1.0, indicating statistical neutrality (no significant increase or decrease). Characterizing the finding as 'actually experienced reduced risk' overstates what was found, implying a statistically proven protective benefit where the evidence shows only neutral effects.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: HHS Cancels $500 Million in mRNA Vaccine Projects, Citing Safety Concerns
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Health and Human Services will cancel contracts and pull funding for some vaccines that are being developed to fight respiratory viruses like COVID-19 and the flu.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced in a statement Tuesday that 22 projects, totaling $500 million, to develop vaccines using mRNA technology will be halted.

Kennedy's decision to terminate the projects is the latest in a string of decisions that have put the longtime vaccine critic's doubts about shots into full effect at the nation's health department. Kennedy has pulled back recommendations around the COVID-19 shots, fired the panel that makes vaccine recommendations, and refused to offer a vigorous endorsement of vaccinations as a measles outbreak worsened.

The health secretary criticized mRNA vaccines in a video on his social media accounts, explaining the decision to cancel projects being led by the nation's leading pharmaceutical companies, including Pfizer and Moderna, that offer protection against viruses like the flu, COVID-19 and H5N1.

"To replace the troubled mRNA programs, we're prioritizing the development of safer, broader vaccine strategies, like whole-virus vaccines and novel platforms that don't collapse when viruses mutate," Kennedy said in the video.

Infectious disease experts say the mRNA technology used in vaccines is safe, and they credit its development during the Biden administration with slowing the 2020 coronavirus pandemic. Future pandemics, they warned, will be harder to stop without the help of mRNA.

"I don't think I've seen a more dangerous decision in public health in my 50 years in the business," said Mike Osterholm, a University of Minnesota expert on infectious diseases and pandemic preparations.

The shelving of the mRNA projects is short-sighted as concerns about a bird flu pandemic continue to loom, said Dr. Paul Offit, a vaccine expert at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.

"It's certainly saved millions of lives," Offit said of the existing mRNA vaccines.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Immigration Courts Become 'Deportation Traps' as Trump Administration Restructures System
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
Associated Press reporters observed immigration court proceedings in 21 cities this year, documenting how hearings repeatedly ended with cases dismissed by the government, allowing agents to arrest immigrants in courthouse hallways.

The scenes are part of a broader makeover of immigration courts under President Trump's second term. In one typical case, a Cuban man who had lived in the United States for years brought his wife and 7-month-old infant to what he thought was a routine hearing. After the government lawyer quickly moved to dismiss his asylum claim, plainclothes immigration agents swarmed him as he left the courtroom.

Screenshots of text messages obtained by AP show coordination between prosecutors and ICE agents. "I can't do this," one government lawyer texted an agent. "This is a new emotional load."

Over the past nine months, the Trump administration has fired almost 90 immigration judges seen as too lenient and sent memos instructing remaining judges to fall into line. Unlike federal courts with lifetime tenure, the Justice Department runs immigration courts and can fire judges with fewer restraints.

Courtehouse arrests are coordinated days in advance using spreadsheets noting which cases are "amenable" to dismissal. Most detained migrants are men without lawyers who don't have criminal convictions, contrary to Trump's claims of targeting the "worst of the worst."

The administration has issued 52 policy memos since January—more than the previous six years combined. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to lend 600 military lawyers to immigration courts, roughly doubling current capacity.

The harsh tactics have driven voluntary departures to soar, with over 14,000 migrants seeking court permission to self-deport in 2025's first eight months—more than the previous five years combined.

Tania Nemer, fired as an immigration judge in February, believes her Arab-sounding name and diversity training contributed to her dismissal. The majority of 86 fired judges were hired under Biden and granted asylum at markedly higher rates than peers.

With $30 million in legal assistance programs eliminated, lawyers now operate from parking lots outside courthouses, helping migrants navigate a system where due process has become "an afterthought."

"In 1934, Congress did guarantee birthright citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States," Salsman said.

Since 1934, federal law has guaranteed Native American citizenship. If Native American citizens are stopped by ICE, they have the right to remain silent and may want to carry Tribal ID, state ID, driver's license, or other forms of identification as evidence of citizenship.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Federal Investigation Finds Native American Mascot Bans Discriminatory as Local Districts Navigate Complex Approval Processes
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
After a three-year process, Minnesota's Deer River Schools received approval for its Native American mascot from the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe in July. The tribal council approved the district's spear and feather design under a 2025 amendment to Minnesota law allowing districts to use American Indian imagery only with formal tribal consent.

"This decision reflects the value of collaboration and honors the intent of the law, which rightly recognizes tribal sovereignty," said Faron Jackson Sr., chairman of the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe.

The approval process became simpler after legislators amended the original 2023 law, which required approval from all 11 federally recognized tribes in the state. Now districts only need approval from their American Indian Parent Advisory Committee and primary tribal partner.

This local resolution comes amid broader federal intervention. The Trump administration's Education Department has launched investigations into New York school districts, finding the state's Native American mascot ban violates Title VI anti-discrimination protections. In May, federal officials determined that prohibiting Indigenous mascots while allowing other cultural imagery constitutes illegal discrimination.

"The Trump Administration will not stand idly by as state leaders attempt to eliminate the history and culture of Native American tribes," said Education Secretary Linda McMahon.

However, research suggests Native American mascots can harm Indigenous students. The American Psychological Association cites studies showing such imagery reduces self-esteem and increases anxiety among Native youth, while boosting self-worth among European Americans.

The Native American Guardians Association, which filed the complaint triggering federal investigation, supports respectful use of Indigenous imagery when done correctly and with tribal input.

Yet the National Indian Education Association opposes most such mascots, arguing they "perpetuate harmful stereotypes and contribute to hostile learning environments for Native students."

In Deer River, where about one-third of students are Native American, avoiding a mascot change saved the district approximately $300,000 in rebranding costs during a period of budget reductions. As of 2023, over 1,900 schools across 21 states still maintain Native-themed mascots.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed the Education Department's position from investigating and claiming discrimination to actually 'finding' that the bans are discriminatory violations of Title VI, making it sound like a concluded legal determination rather than an ongoing investigation and claim

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Trump Administration Investigates Health Systems Over Religious Exemptions for Gender-Affirming Care
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
Federal health officials are investigating the University of Michigan Health system after a former employee claimed she was fired for seeking a religious exemption from providing gender-affirming care.[source article excerpt omitted]former employee Valerie Kloosterman[source article excerpt omitted].

The probes are the first time HHS is applying those amendments in a way that would "allow providers to refuse gender-affirming care or to misgender patients," said Elizabeth Sepper, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law who studies conscience laws. Those laws, Sepper said, primarily allow objections to performing abortions or sterilizations.

Kloosterman worked as a physician assistant at University of Michigan Health-West when she participated in mandatory diversity training in 2021. According to her 2022 federal lawsuit, the health system required her to pledge she would use preferred pronouns and make referrals for gender transition procedures, which conflicted with her religious beliefs.

When Kloosterman requested a religious accommodation, administrators allegedly called her "evil" and a "liar" before firing her in August 2021. The health system denied these allegations, arguing they would not require employees to provide care that conflicted with their beliefs, but expected non-discriminatory treatment of all patients.

In April 2024, U.S. District Judge Jane Beckering ruled the case should be settled in private arbitration. Kloosterman has appealed to the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals.

The Church Amendments from the 1970s allow healthcare providers to refuse participation in abortion or sterilization procedures, but legal experts say applying them to gender-affirming care represents a significant expansion of their original scope.

claims.reasoning: Confirmed: HHS described the Michigan probe as the third in a larger effort to enforce conscience and religious exercise protections for medical providers under the Church Amendments.

claims.text: Elizabeth Sepper, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law, said the HHS probes are the first time the Church Amendments are being applied to allow providers to refuse gender-affirming care, noting the laws primarily allow objections to abortions or sterilizations.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Elizabeth Sepper, law professor at UT Austin who studies conscience laws, stated these are the first HHS applications of the Church Amendments to gender-affirming care refusals, and that the laws primarily cover abortion and sterilization objections.

The rewrite omits the word 'dismissed,' changing the ruling from a case dismissal (which sends the case to arbitration by removing it from court) to simply an order for arbitration, which misrepresents the nature of the judicial action. The dismissal was later overturned on appeal by the 6th Circuit in August 2025.

claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The Church Amendments date to the 1970s and their core provisions allow healthcare institutions and providers to refuse to participate in abortion or sterilization procedures.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Federal Judge Blocks Trump Administration's End to Temporary Protected Status for Haiti and Venezuela
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
A federal judge on Friday blocked the Trump administration from ending temporary legal protections that have granted more than 1 million people from Haiti and Venezuela the right to live and work in the United States.

The ruling by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen of San Francisco[source article excerpt omitted]Temporary Protected Status is a designation that can be granted by the Homeland Security secretary to people in the United States, if conditions in their homelands are deemed unsafe for return due to natural disasters, political instability or other dangerous conditions.

Millions of Venezuelans have fled political unrest, mass unemployment and hunger. Haiti was first designated for TPS in 2015 after widespread gang violence and political instability destabilized the country. Haitians continue to face widespread hunger and violence.

Noem said that conditions in both Haiti and Venezuela had improved and that it was not in the national interest to allow migrants from the countries to stay on for what is a temporary program.

The secretary's action in revoking TPS was not only unprecedented in the manner and speed in which it was taken but also violated the law, Chen wrote.

The government is expected to appeal the ruling.
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: Haiti was first designated for TPS in 2015 after widespread gang violence and political instability
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed Haiti's first TPS designation from 2010 after a catastrophic magnitude 7.0 earthquake to 2015 after gang violence and political instability. This is false - Haiti was actually first designated for TPS in 2010 following the devastating earthquake.

claims.text: U.S. District Judge Edward Chen of San Francisco blocked the Trump administration from ending TPS, preserving protections for 600,000 Venezuelans and 500,000 Haitians.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Judge Edward Chen issued a ruling on September 6, 2025 blocking the Trump administration's termination of TPS for Haiti and Venezuela, covering approximately 600,000 Venezuelans and 500,000 Haitians.

claims.text: Chen said Noem's actions were arbitrary and capricious, and she exceeded her authority in ending protections that were extended by the Biden administration.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Judge Chen ruled that Noem's actions in terminating and vacating TPS extensions granted by the Biden administration were arbitrary and capricious and exceeded her statutory authority.

claims.text: Chen wrote that presidential administrations have executed the law for 35 years in 'a process that involves careful study and analysis. Until now.'
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Judge Chen's written ruling included this characterization of how prior administrations handled TPS designations, contrasting it with the Trump administration's approach.

claims.text: Haiti was first designated for TPS in 2015 after widespread gang violence and political instability destabilized the country.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered claim. Haiti was first designated for TPS in January 2010 — not 2015 — following the catastrophic magnitude 7.0 earthquake that struck on January 12, 2010. The Obama administration designated TPS for Haiti on January 15, 2010, just three days after the earthquake. The article changed both the year (2010→2015) and the triggering event (earthquake→gang violence/political instability).

claims.text: TPS is a designation that can be granted by the Homeland Security secretary to people in the United States if conditions in their homelands are deemed unsafe for return due to natural disasters, political instability or other dangerous conditions.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: This accurately describes the legal basis for TPS under 8 U.S.C. § 1254a — the DHS Secretary may designate a country for TPS if conditions are unsafe due to ongoing armed conflict, environmental disaster, or other extraordinary and temporary conditions.

claims.text: Noem said conditions in both Haiti and Venezuela had improved and it was not in the national interest to allow migrants to stay on for what is a temporary program.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Kristi Noem cited improved conditions in Haiti and Venezuela and national interest grounds as justification for terminating TPS designations.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: The Associated Press is the real global news agency that reported on Judge Chen's TPS ruling. The contact 'Immigration Reporter, AP' is a generic team identifier with no personal name or email address, consistent with AP's byline practices for breaking news.

U.S. District Judge Edward Chen of the Northern District of California (San Francisco) is the real federal judge who issued the TPS ruling blocking the Trump administration's termination of protections for Venezuelans and Haitians on September 6, 2025.
Kristi Noem is the real DHS Secretary whose actions in terminating TPS for Venezuela and Haiti were blocked by Judge Chen's September 2025 ruling.
DHS is the real U.S. federal department whose Secretary is responsible for TPS designations and whose actions were challenged in the Chen ruling.

All sources non-empty.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: Rewrite article #98 on the TPS judicial review contains one deliberately altered historical fact. All other claims are accurate: Judge Edward Chen's September 6, 2025 ruling blocking TPS termination for 600,000 Venezuelans and 500,000 Haitians confirmed; Chen's 'arbitrary and capricious' ruling on Noem confirmed; '35 years...until now' quote confirmed; TPS definition confirmed; Noem's improved-conditions rationale confirmed. The introduced misinformation: Haiti's first TPS designation was changed from '2010 after a catastrophic magnitude 7.0 earthquake' to '2015 after widespread gang violence and political instability.' Haiti was designated for TPS on January 15, 2010 — just three days after the devastating January 12, 2010 earthquake — under the Obama administration. The change shifts both the date (by 5 years) and the triggering event (earthquake to gang violence), replacing a well-documented historical fact. No fabricated contacts or entities: contact 'Immigration Reporter, AP' is a generic team identifier with no personal name or email.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: HHS Report on Pediatric Gender Care Draws Medical Community Criticism
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) released a final version of its report on pediatric gender-affirming care on Wednesday, claiming it found "medical dangers posed to children," which is receiving pushback from medical groups.

The report alleged that gender-affirming care -- including puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and gender-affirming surgeries -- caused significant, long-term damage.

It comes after HHS published in May an early version of what it referred to as a "comprehensive review" of transgender care for children and teens, in which it called for a broader use of psychotherapy for young people with gender dysphoria rather than gender-affirming medical interventions[source article excerpt omitted]In a press release on Wednesday, Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, called the report "a turning point for American medicine," adding that "we are committed to ensuring that science, not ideology, guides America's medical research."

The final version of the HHS report listed nine authors, all of whom have expressed skeptical views of, or have opposed, pediatric gender-affirming care. The disclosures show that at least six of the nine authors have financial interests or have spoken out extensively opposing gender affirming care.

Gender-affirming care is supported by multiple major medical organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society. Studies have shown that many of the treatment options are generally safe and that care can have a positive impact on mental health.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Conservative Parties Secure Major Victories in Japan and Thailand Snap Elections
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
Incumbent conservative parties won sweeping victories in Japan and Thailand's snap elections yesterday, strengthening their respective mandates. In Japan, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) clinched a supermajority in the lower legislative house. In Thailand, preliminary results showed Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul's Bhumjaithai Party winning around 194 seats in the country's 500-person lower house, while opposition progressives secured only around 116.

In Japan, Takaichi took a gamble by holding a snap election just 110 days after taking office. The LDP's congressional strength had lagged in recent years, forcing it to rely on coalition partners to form a government. Ahead of the weekend vote, Takaichi had pledged tougher policies on immigration and China, a boost in government spending, and efforts to change Japan's constitution to empower the country's self-defense forces. Takaichi has underscored the importance of the U.S.-Japan relationship, and U.S. President Donald Trump endorsed her and celebrated her party's victory.

In Thailand, the conservative Bhumjaithai Party defied polls that favored the progressive opposition People's Party, which is popular among young voters and has surged in recent years. Bhumjaithai promotes Thai nationalism and respect for the monarchy. Its popularity rose following Thailand's military clashes with Vietnam last year, paving the way for Anutin to run on a platform of military strength. Bhumjaithai's conservative allies won enough legislative seats to enable a governing coalition.

"[In Japan, Takaichi] can set the legislative agenda and decide what comes up and what doesn't…This is a Takaichi win, but it's not necessarily an LDP win," noted political analyst Kenji Yamamoto.

Both victories signal a broader conservative shift in Southeast Asia, with voters responding to nationalist messaging amid regional security concerns. The results are expected to influence upcoming elections across the region.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Uganda Imposes Internet Blackout Ahead of Presidential Elections
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
Ugandan authorities have imposed a nationwide internet blackout days before presidential elections in which President Yoweri Museveni is expected to prolong his 35-year rule.

A government regulatory body instructed mobile network operators to block public internet access starting at 6pm (15:00 GMT) on Tuesday. Internet monitor NetBlocks later confirmed a "nation-scale disruption to internet connectivity".

The network outage has heightened concerns about repression in the run-up to the January 15 vote, in which 76-year-old Museveni, Africa's third-longest-serving leader, is being challenged [source article excerpt omitted].

The United Nations Human Rights Office has criticised Uganda's authorities for creating an environment of "widespread repression and intimidation" before the vote.

Brussels-based International Crisis Group has assessed that Museveni, "with his firm grip on the levers of state power … has re-election all but locked down."

Wine views his candidacy as a campaign "against impunity," reported Al Jazeera's Catherine Soi from Kampala, Uganda. But "he doesn't believe that he is going to get a free or fair election."

Museveni's government said security forces are acting to stop what it described as lawless conduct by opposition supporters. The Uganda Communications Commission defended the internet shutdown as necessary to "curb misinformation, disinformation, electoral fraud and related risks."

In addition to cutting off the internet, the government on Tuesday ordered two local rights groups that have been critical of authorities to halt their work.

Uganda also blocked internet access during its last election in 2016 – a vote marred by reports of state violence and electoral manipulation.

claims.reasoning: These figures are deliberately altered. The correct facts are that Museveni is 81 years old (born September 1944, age 81 in January 2026) and has ruled for 40 years (having taken power in January 1986). The article reduced his age by 5 years and his length of rule by 5 years. NPR and other sources confirm Museveni, 81, was extending his 'four-decade grip on power' through the 2026 election.

claims.reasoning: Confirmed: NetBlocks confirmed the nationwide internet disruption in Uganda ahead of the January 15, 2026 election, and the Uganda Communications Commission issued the order to mobile operators.

claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The UN Human Rights Office issued criticism of Uganda's pre-election environment, citing widespread repression and intimidation of opposition figures and supporters.

claims.reasoning: This is a deliberately altered date. Uganda's most recent election before 2026 was in 2021 — not 2016. Uganda blocked internet access during its 2021 election, not 2016. The article changed '2021' to '2016,' making it appear the previous internet shutdown happened a decade earlier.

claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Bobi Wine (Robert Kyagulanyi), the pop star-turned-politician, challenged Museveni in the 2026 Uganda presidential election, finishing second with 24.72% of votes.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Trump's Greenland Push Looms Over Parliamentary Election
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
President Donald Trump[source article excerpt omitted] [source article excerpt omitted]Since the beginning of his second term in the White House, Trump has repeatedly called for the annexation of Greenland and negotiations with Denmark -- which the country has denied.

"We need Greenland for national security and even international security," Trump said during his joint address to Congress last week.

A recent poll of Greenland residents found that 67% of respondents did not wish to join the U.S. Additionally, 56% of those polled said they would vote for independence from Denmark if a referendum were to be held.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed the poll result from 85% of Greenlanders opposing joining the U.S. to 67%, making Trump's annexation goals appear more viable than they actually are

claims.text: Greenland, an autonomous territory in the Kingdom of Denmark, has approximately 41,000 registered voters.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Wikipedia reports 40,369 registered voters for the 2025 Greenlandic general election — 'approximately 41,000' is an accurate approximation.

claims.text: Its last election was held in 2021.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Greenland's previous parliamentary election before the 2025 election was held on April 6, 2021.

claims.text: The election was comprised of six political parties vying for control of Greenland's parliament, known as the Inatsisartut. Among those parties, 31 lawmakers will be elected to leadership Tuesday.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Six parties participated in the 2025 Greenlandic election, and the Inatsisartut has 31 seats elected by open list proportional representation.

claims.text: The world's largest island has been under Danish rule for over 300 years, but it gained autonomous leadership in 1979.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Greenland achieved home rule in 1979 and has been under Danish rule for over 300 years.

claims.text: Greenland Prime Minister Múte Egede called Tuesday's election a 'fateful choice' for the Arctic region.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Greenland Prime Minister Múte Egede framed the 2025 election as a 'fateful choice,' widely reported by NPR and other outlets.

claims.text: That movement has been led by Egede and the ruling party, the democratic socialist Inuit Ataqatigiit.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Inuit Ataqatigiit is described as advocating democratic socialism and was the governing party heading into the 2025 election under Múte Egede.

claims.text: A recent poll of Greenland residents found that 67% of respondents did not wish to join the U.S.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered statistic. The actual poll (Verian Group, January 2025, 497 respondents) found that 85% of Greenlanders did not wish to join the U.S., with only 6% in favor and 9% unsure. The article reduced 85% to 67%, making Trump's annexation goal appear far more viable than polling actually suggests.

claims.text: 56% of those polled said they would vote for independence from Denmark if a referendum were to be held.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The same Verian Group poll found 56% would vote yes to independence if a referendum were held, 28% no, and 17% unsure.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Myanmar Military Stages Elections Amid Civil War as International Support Grows
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]2021 coup[source article excerpt omitted]To ensure the elections go its way, the military has introduced a new law that bans what it calls "interference" in the election process. Human Rights Watch said in November that nearly 100 people had been detained under the law. By last week, the military said that number had more than doubled, some charged for posting on social media criticizing the election process.

Most Western governments have refused to send observers, denouncing the election as a "sham." Critics say the military is trying to create a parliament dominated by the military's proxy party, the Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP). The NLD is banned this time around, with Aung San Suu Kyi and other party leaders remaining in prison.

The junta has gotten significant help from neighboring China and Russia — both countries endorsing the election, along with India, Thailand, and Vietnam. China doesn't like the Myanmar military or its coup, but dislikes the chaos that's followed even more, says Yun Sun, who directs the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, D.C.

After nearly five years of war, economic hardship and displacement, many Burmese simply want anything that offers hope of relief. There's a growing sense among citizens that while they hate the regime, at least it has a plan to stabilize the country, says longtime Myanmar analyst David Mathieson.
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.claim: India, Thailand, and Vietnam have endorsed Myanmar's military election
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.changesMade: Changed the statement that only China, Russia, and 'to a lesser extent, India' endorsed the election to falsely claim that India, Thailand, and Vietnam have all endorsed it, significantly overstating international support for the junta's election

claims.text: Myanmar's military rulers are holding a staggered general election beginning Dec. 28 and ending in late January.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: The 2025-26 Myanmar general election began on December 28, 2025 in three phases, concluding on January 25, 2026.

claims.text: The vote is taking place despite a brutal, ongoing civil war that followed the military's 2021 coup.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Myanmar's military carried out a coup on February 1, 2021, leading to an ongoing civil war that was still raging during the December 2025 election.

claims.text: Aid agencies say more than 11 million people are facing food insecurity.
claims.reasoning: Supported: While more recent data (2025) shows food insecurity escalating to ~15 million, the 'more than 11 million' figure is a lower-bound understatement that is technically accurate. The UN and WFP have consistently reported food insecurity above 11 million since 2023.

claims.text: Human Rights Watch said in November that nearly 100 people had been detained under the law. By last week, the military said that number had more than doubled.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Human Rights Watch reported arrests under Myanmar's election interference law ahead of the December 2025 vote, with the junta reporting growing detention figures as it clamped down on election critics.

claims.text: Critics say the military is trying to create a parliament dominated by the military's proxy party, the Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP). The NLD is banned this time around, with Aung San Suu Kyi and other party leaders remaining in prison.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: USDP is the military's proxy party; the NLD was banned and Suu Kyi remained in prison. USDP achieved overwhelming victory, winning 231 seats in the House of Representatives and 108 in the House of Nationalities.

claims.text: The junta has gotten significant help from neighboring China and Russia — both countries endorsing the election, along with India, Thailand, and Vietnam.
claims.reasoning: This is the deliberately altered claim. The original article stated that China endorsed the election 'along with Russia and, to a lesser extent, neighboring India' — explicitly limiting endorsement to those three. The rewrite adds Thailand and Vietnam as explicit endorsers alongside China and Russia. While India, Cambodia, and Vietnam sent observers (a lesser form of legitimation), Thailand is not reported as endorsing or sending observers. More importantly, the 'to a lesser extent' qualifier for India is dropped, and the framing upgrades Vietnam from 'observer' to full endorser. Wikipedia only mentions India as a prospective observer, not Thailand or Vietnam as endorsers.

claims.text: Yun Sun, who directs the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, D.C.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: Yun Sun is Senior Fellow and Director of the China Program at the Stimson Center in Washington, D.C., with expertise in Chinese foreign policy and Myanmar-China relations.

claims.text: There's a growing sense among citizens that while they hate the regime, at least it has a plan to stabilize the country, says longtime Myanmar analyst David Mathieson.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed: David Scott Mathieson is a real longtime Myanmar analyst who has written extensively on Myanmar's civil war, human rights, and the junta's political strategies for the Lowy Institute, Asia Times, and other outlets.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: The Associated Press is the real global news agency, headquartered in New York, that reported on Myanmar's military election.

No email address is provided, making domain verification impossible. WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court will hear arguments over the Trump administration'[source article excerpt omitted]'s wider crackdown on immigration.

The case will be heard in April, a fast schedule for the nation's highest court, with a decision expected weeks or months later.

The conservative-majority court has sided with the Trump administration on the issue before and allowed the end of temporary legal status for a total of 600,000 people from Venezuela while lawsuits play out, exposing them to potential deportation.

The Trump administration filed emergency appeals after lower courts stopped the immediate end of the program for 350,000 people from Haiti and 6,000 people from Syria.

The Justice Department argued that the Department of Homeland Security has sole power over the program, which was designed to be temporary.

"Lower courts are again attempting to block major executive-branch policy initiatives in ways that inflict specific harms to the national interest and foreign relations," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in court documents.

But immigration attorneys argued that both countries are still largely in crisis and people can't return safely.

"Without a functioning government, Haiti is a nation in turmoil. Rape, kidnapping, and murder are rampant, while food, housing, and medical care are scarce," attorneys wrote.

Courts in New York and Washington, D.C., have agreed to delay the end of protections, with one finding that "hostility to nonwhite immigrants" likely played a role in the decision.

A total of about 1.3 million people fleeing armed conflict, natural disasters and political instability have been granted temporary protected status. The protections for Haitians were first granted in 2010 after a catastrophic earthquake, while protections for Syrians were first granted in 2012 during civil war.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Zelenskyy Ready for Peace Talks as Iran War Diverts Global Attention
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in comments released Sunday that he was ready for the next round of trilateral peace talks to end Russia's more than 4-year-old invasion of Ukraine, but that it was up to Washington and Moscow to agree on where and when to meet.

Zelenskyy said the U.S. had proposed hosting the next meeting between American, Ukrainian and Russian negotiating teams, which include U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, but Moscow had refused to send a delegation.

"We are waiting for a response from the Americans. Either they will change the country where we meet, or the Russians must confirm the U.S," Zelenskyy said in a media briefing Saturday. "We are not blocking any of these initiatives. We want a trilateral meeting to take place."

The U.S. has postponed its sponsored talks between the two sides due to the war in the Middle East. The Iran war, which erupted on Feb. 28 following Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in Jordan and spread across the region, has drawn the international spotlight away from Ukraine's plight as it strives to hold back Russia's bigger army.

Speaking to journalists, Zelenskyy also warned of a "very high" risk that the Iran war could drain the air defense stockpiles Ukraine depends on to counter Russian missile strikes. He said he lacked a clear picture of available stockpiles and had discussed with French President Emmanuel Macron whether SAMP/T systems could serve as alternatives to U.S.-made Patriot batteries.

Regarding the Druzhba pipeline, which until late January transported Russian oil to Hungary and Slovakia, Zelenskyy said he opposed allowing Russian oil transit through Ukraine while the EU imposes sanctions elsewhere. Oil deliveries have been halted since Jan. 27, leading to disputes between Hungary and Ukraine. Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has vetoed new EU sanctions against Russia and is blocking a major 90-billion euro EU loan for Ukraine until flows resume.

anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.headline: Ukraine-Russia Peace Talks in Geneva End Without Breakthrough as War's Fourth Anniversary Nears
anthropic__claude-sonnet-4/misinfoqa/rew.body:
GENEVA (AP) — The latest U.S.-brokered talks between envoys from Moscow and Kyiv over Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine ended Wednesday with no sign of a breakthrough and with both sides saying the talks were "difficult," as the war's fourth anniversary approaches next week.

The negotiations in Switzerland were the third round of direct talks organized by the U.S., after meetings earlier this year in Abu Dhabi that officials described as constructive but which also made no major headway. Expectations for significant progress in Geneva were low.

"The negotiations were not easy," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after the talks broke up and he spoke briefly by phone from Kyiv with his negotiating team[source article excerpt omitted]"were difficult but businesslike."

Zelenskyy described the military discussions as "constructive," adding that the armed forces of both countries considered how any future ceasefire might be monitored. "Monitoring will definitely be carried out with participation of the Chinese side," he said in a voice message shared in a media group chat on WhatsApp.

U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, said on social media that Washington's push for peace in Ukraine over the past year has "brought about meaningful progress," without elaborating.

The two armies remain locked in battle on the roughly 1,250-kilometer (750-mile) front line, while Russia bombards civilian areas of Ukraine daily. Overnight, Russia launched one ballistic missile and 126 long-range drones at Ukraine, according to the Ukrainian air force.

Russia and Ukraine appear to still be far apart on their demands for a settlement. Putin's key goals remain what he declared when Russia invaded its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022: Ukraine must renounce joining NATO, sharply reduce the size of its army and protect Russian language and culture.
